cue: Describe a piece of technology you find useful.
closing: and explain why you find it so useful.
followUps: Is there any technology you find annoying?
sampleAnswer: The piece of technology I'd like to talk about is a pair of noise-cancelling headphones that I bought about two years ago. I'd been saving up for a while, because they weren't cheap, and I finally bought them just before my second-year exams, which turned out to be perfect timing. They're over-ear headphones, dark grey, and they fold up into a small case, so I can carry them in my backpack everywhere. I use them pretty much every single day. In the morning I put them on during my bus journey, and they block out the engine noise and other people's conversations, so I can listen to podcasts or just enjoy some quiet. At the library, or at home when my flatmates are being loud, I use them while I study, sometimes with music and sometimes with nothing playing at all, just to create silence. I also use them for video calls with my family, because the microphone is surprisingly clear. The reason I find them so useful is that they basically give me control over my environment. I live in a noisy part of the city and share a flat with two people, so finding peace and quiet isn't easy. Before I had them, I really struggled to concentrate, and I'd often end up wasting an afternoon because of noise. Now I can create my own quiet space wherever I am. I'm convinced they've made me more productive, and they've also made me less stressed, because constant noise is surprisingly exhausting. The only downside is that sometimes I forget I'm wearing them and don't hear people talking to me, which has led to a few embarrassing moments, like completely ignoring my flatmate when she asked me a question.

topic: A film or documentary that taught you something
cue: Describe a film or documentary that taught you something.
bullets: what it was called or what it was about
when and where you watched it
closing: and explain why it made an impression on you.
followUps: Do you prefer documentaries or fiction films?
Did you talk about it with anyone afterwards?
sampleAnswer: I'd like to talk about a documentary I watched last year about the ocean, and specifically about the life of coral reefs. I watched it on a streaming platform one rainy Sunday afternoon with my flatmate, and honestly, we only chose it because we couldn't agree on a film. The documentary followed a team of scientists over several years as they studied reefs in different parts of the world. It showed how incredibly rich these ecosystems are, with thousands of species depending on each other, and it explained in a very clear way how rising sea temperatures cause something called coral bleaching, where the corals lose the algae that give them their colour and food. There were some heartbreaking scenes where they filmed the same reef before and after a heatwave, and it went from bright and full of fish to completely white and almost empty. What I learned, apart from the science, was how quickly environmental damage can happen. I had always thought of climate change as something slow and abstract, something that would affect people in fifty years. But here was clear evidence of huge changes happening in just a few months. On the positive side, the documentary also showed projects where people are growing corals in nurseries and replanting them, which gave me some hope. The reason it made such an impression on me was probably the visual contrast. Statistics are easy to ignore, but seeing a living reef turn into something that looked like a graveyard was really powerful. Afterwards, my flatmate and I talked about it for ages, and it actually led me to change a few habits, like eating less meat and flying less. It also made me want to learn to dive, so I can see a reef with my own eyes before it's too late.

cue: Describe a time when you helped someone.
closing: and explain how you felt about helping this person.
followUps: Do you think people in your city help strangers?
sampleAnswer: I'd like to talk about a time I helped an elderly tourist who was completely lost at a train station. This happened about a year ago at the main station in my city, on a busy Friday evening. I was rushing to catch a train home for the weekend when I noticed an old man standing in the middle of the hall, looking at a printed ticket and then at the departure boards, clearly confused. People were just rushing past him. I had about fifteen minutes before my train, so I went over and asked if he needed help. It turned out he was from Japan, and he spoke very little English and no Spanish at all, so communication was a bit of a challenge. With a combination of gestures, a translation app on my phone, and pointing at his ticket, I worked out that his train had been moved to a different platform, which had been announced only in Spanish. On top of that, the platform was in a separate part of the station, down an escalator that was out of order. So I carried his suitcase down the stairs, walked him to the right platform, and checked with a member of staff that it was the correct train. He was so grateful that he bowed several times and insisted on giving me a small keyring shaped like a cat, which I still have on my backpack. I did miss my own train, so I had to wait an hour for the next one, but I honestly didn't mind. I felt really good about it, partly because it was such a simple thing to do, and partly because I could imagine how scared I'd feel lost in a foreign country. It reminded me that small acts of kindness can make a huge difference to someone's day.

cue: Describe a sports event that you watched or took part in.
bullets: where and when it took place
closing: and explain why this event was memorable.
followUps: Do you prefer watching sports live or on TV?
sampleAnswer: The event I'd like to describe is a half-marathon that I ran in my city last spring. It was the first long-distance race I'd ever taken part in, and it took place on a Sunday morning in April, starting at eight o'clock in front of the city hall. About five thousand people took part, from serious athletes to people in fancy dress. I ran it with my cousin, Marta, who's a much more experienced runner than me. She'd convinced me to sign up about four months earlier, and we'd trained together three times a week, gradually building up from short runs to about eighteen kilometres. On the day itself, the atmosphere was incredible. The streets were lined with people cheering, there were bands playing music at different points along the route, and children were holding out their hands for high fives. The first ten kilometres felt surprisingly easy, mainly because of all the adrenaline. But around the fifteenth kilometre, I hit a wall. My legs felt like concrete, and I seriously considered walking. Marta could easily have gone ahead and got a better time, but she stayed with me, kept talking to me, and made me focus on reaching the next water station. When we turned the final corner and saw the finish line, I somehow found the energy to sprint, and we crossed it together in just over two hours. It was memorable for several reasons. Firstly, it was a real personal achievement, because a year earlier I couldn't even run five kilometres. Secondly, it showed me how much support from others matters. And finally, the feeling of the whole city coming together for a day was really special. I'm now training for my second one, and this time I'm aiming to finish under two hours.

cue: Describe a historical place that you have visited.
bullets: what you saw and did there
closing: and explain how you felt about visiting this place.
followUps: Would you recommend this place to tourists?
Do you enjoy learning about history?
sampleAnswer: I'd like to talk about the Roman ruins of an ancient city I visited in the south of Portugal about three years ago, during a road trip with some friends. It's not one of the famous sites that everyone has heard of, which is probably why it made such a strong impression on me. We arrived early in the morning, before it got too hot, and we were almost the only visitors there. The site is on a small hill overlooking a river valley, and you walk around on a dusty path between the remains of houses, a public bathhouse and what used to be the forum, the main square of the town. Most of the walls are only knee-high now, but you can still clearly see the layout of the rooms. The most amazing thing was the mosaics. Several of the houses still have their original floors, with intricate patterns and images of fish, birds and geometric shapes, all made from tiny coloured stones. There was also a small museum at the entrance with everyday objects found on the site, things like oil lamps, hairpins, coins and even a child's toy. Honestly, I felt quite emotional being there. Standing in someone's living room, looking at the floor they would have walked on two thousand years ago, made history feel very real and personal in a way that textbooks never did for me. Those everyday objects, especially the toy, reminded me that the people who lived there weren't so different from us. It also made me reflect on how temporary everything is. A whole thriving town had been completely abandoned and forgotten. Since that trip, I've become much more interested in archaeology, and I've visited quite a few other sites, but none of them have quite matched that first experience.

topic: A time you were very busy
cue: Describe a time when you were very busy.
closing: and explain how you felt during this busy period.
followUps: Do you work better under pressure?
sampleAnswer: The busiest period of my life so far was probably the final month of my undergraduate degree, about a year and a half ago. It was a perfect storm, really. I had to submit my final dissertation, which was about forty pages long and worth a huge part of my grade. At the same time, I had four final exams, and I was working twenty hours a week in a bookshop to pay my rent. As if that weren't enough, I was also moving out of my flat at the end of the month, so I had to pack everything and find somewhere new to live. At the beginning, I panicked a bit, and I wasted a couple of days just feeling overwhelmed. Then I sat down and made a detailed plan. I listed every single task and deadline, and I worked backwards from each one. I divided my days into blocks, so mornings were for the dissertation, afternoons for exam revision, and evenings for work or packing. I also had to learn to say no. I turned down invitations to parties and even asked my manager at the bookshop to reduce my hours for two weeks, which he kindly agreed to. My flatmates helped too; we took turns cooking so that nobody had to cook every day. As for how I felt, it was a real mix. A lot of the time I was exhausted and stressed, and I remember a few nights where I lay awake worrying about everything I still had to do. But there was also a strange sense of satisfaction every time I ticked something off my list. When I finally handed in my dissertation, two days early, I felt incredibly proud. It taught me that I'm capable of much more than I think, but also that I never want to be that busy again.

cue: Describe a gift you gave to someone.
closing: and explain how the person felt about the gift.
followUps: Do you find it easy to choose presents for people?
sampleAnswer: I'd like to talk about a gift I gave my father for his sixtieth birthday last year. It was a photo book that I made myself, which told the story of his life through pictures. I chose it because my dad is notoriously difficult to buy presents for. Whenever you ask him what he wants, he says he doesn't need anything, and he's the kind of person who never uses gadgets or wears new clothes. But I knew he's quite sentimental, and I also knew that our family photos were scattered everywhere, in old albums, in boxes in the attic and on different people's phones. So I thought it would be meaningful to bring them all together. The process took me about two months. I secretly borrowed old albums from my grandmother and scanned the photos, and I contacted his brothers and some of his old friends to ask for pictures and short anecdotes. Some of them sent hilarious photos of my dad as a teenager with very long hair, which none of us had ever seen. Then I arranged everything chronologically, from his childhood in a small village to his wedding, the birth of my sister and me, and recent family holidays. Under some of the photos, I added the little stories his friends had sent. When he opened it at his birthday dinner, he went very quiet. He turned the pages slowly, and at one point he had to take off his glasses and wipe his eyes, which I'd never seen him do before. Then he started laughing and telling stories about every single photo, and the whole family gathered round. He told me later it was the best present he'd ever received. It sits on the coffee table in the living room now, and apparently he shows it to every visitor.

topic: A famous person you would like to meet
cue: Describe a famous person you would like to meet.
bullets: what you would like to do or talk about with them
closing: and explain why you would like to meet this person.
followUps: Do you think famous people have an easy life?
sampleAnswer: The famous person I'd love to meet is a well-known marine biologist, a scientist who spent decades studying whales in the wild and later became a campaigner for ocean protection. I first heard about her when I was about twelve, when we watched a documentary about her work at school. I was fascinated by the idea of a young woman heading out to sea in a tiny boat with just a notebook and an underwater microphone, in an era when very few women were scientists. Since then, I've read one of her books and watched several of her talks online. If I met her, I'd love to ask her about those early years at sea. I'd like to know what it was like to spend months waiting for the whales to get used to her boat, and whether she ever felt lonely or wanted to give up. I'd also ask her how she found the energy to keep going in her campaigns, because she has travelled constantly for decades to give talks, even in her eighties. And honestly, I'd just love to go out on a boat with her and hear her describe what she notices, because I imagine she sees things the rest of us completely miss. There are a few reasons why she's the person I'd choose. Firstly, she changed the way people understand animals. Her recordings helped to show that whales communicate in remarkably complex ways, which was revolutionary at the time. Secondly, she's an example of how one person's curiosity can turn into something that benefits the whole planet. And finally, she's famous for being hopeful, even about huge problems like climate change. Sometimes I feel quite pessimistic about the future, so I think talking to someone like her would be genuinely inspiring and might change my outlook.

topic: A website or app you use often
cue: Describe a website or app that you use often.
bullets: how you found out about it
closing: and explain why you use it so often.
followUps: Do you think you spend too much time online?
Would you pay for this app or website?
sampleAnswer: The app I'd like to talk about is a language learning app that I've been using almost every day for about three years. I found out about it from a friend at university who was learning Japanese and kept showing off the little cartoon characters and the streak counter that tracks how many days in a row you've studied. At first, I thought it was just a game, but I downloaded it to brush up on my Italian before a trip, and I've been hooked ever since. Basically, the app gives you short lessons, each one taking about five or ten minutes. You translate sentences, match words with pictures, listen to audio clips, and sometimes speak into the microphone so that it can check your pronunciation. As you progress, the lessons get more complex, and there are also short stories and podcasts for higher levels. I use it mainly for Italian, but recently I've started learning some basic Korean as well, just for fun. The main reason I use it so often is that it fits perfectly into the gaps in my day. I usually do a lesson on the bus in the morning and another one while I'm waiting for my coffee or before bed. It doesn't feel like studying, because it's designed like a game, with points, levels and competitions with friends. I'll admit the streak counter is a big motivator; my current streak is over seven hundred days, and I'd be heartbroken if I lost it. Of course, I'm aware that an app alone won't make me fluent. When I went to Italy last summer, I realised my listening was still weak in real conversations. But it's a great way to keep my languages active, and it has definitely made learning a daily habit.

topic: A skill you would like to learn
cue: Describe a skill you would like to learn in the future.
bullets: how difficult you think it would be
closing: and explain why you would like to learn this skill.
followUps: Do you think adults learn new skills as easily as children?
sampleAnswer: One skill I'd really like to learn in the future is sign language, specifically the sign language used in my country. The idea first came to me about a year ago, when a deaf student joined one of my seminars at university. She had an interpreter with her, and I was fascinated watching them, but I also felt a bit awkward because I couldn't communicate with her directly, apart from a few written notes. Since then I've noticed how often deaf people are excluded from ordinary conversations, and I'd like to be able to do something about it, even in a small way. As for how I'd learn it, I think the best approach would be to take a proper course. There's an association for deaf people in my city that runs evening classes taught by deaf teachers, which I think is important, because they can teach the culture as well as the language. I'd combine that with online videos to practise at home, and ideally I'd try to attend some of the social events they organise, so I could practise with fluent signers. I imagine it would be quite difficult, at least at the beginning. It's a completely different way of using language, where facial expressions and the space around you have grammatical meaning, not just your hands. I've read that it has its own grammar, which is very different from spoken language, so I'd need to avoid simply translating word for word. And because I'm used to learning languages through listening, I suspect my visual memory will need a lot of training. The main reason I want to learn it is inclusion. I'd love to be someone who can make others feel welcome. Also, I'm planning to work in healthcare, so it could be genuinely useful professionally, for example when patients need to explain their symptoms.
